subtopic_detail: Medical admission thresholds in anorexia nervosa
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 17 year old woman brought in by her mother after her general practitioner faxed a referral requesting admission for restrictive eating over 8 months. She has been drinking water only for the past two days before a school swimming carnival.

She is alert, tearful and denies feeling unwell. She has no chest pain and no syncope. She takes no regular medications and has never purged.

Weight 41.2 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 15.1). Pulse 38 regular supine, blood pressure 96/58 supine falling to 78/48 on standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius. Peripheral capillary refill 3 seconds and fingers dusky. Venous blood gas: pH 7.42, potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), glucose 3.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 regular, BP 96/58 supine to 78/48 standing, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient dietitian and community eating disorder team follow up within 48 hours
options.rationale: Bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic, hypothermia and hypokalaemia each independently trigger inpatient medical admission under RANZCP and NSW ANZAED criteria; outpatient management is unsafe here (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Commence oral high energy supplements in ED and reassess for admission after 24 hours of ambulatory monitoring
options.rationale: Refeeding in a severely malnourished young person must occur in a monitored inpatient setting with electrolyte replacement to avoid refeeding syndrome; ambulatory refeeding under these vitals is unsafe (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

options.text: Refer directly to a specialist eating disorders inpatient unit and delay any refeeding until formal admission
options.rationale: Specialist eating disorder beds have long wait lists and she is medically unstable now; medical stabilisation on the nearest paediatric or adolescent ward with cardiac monitoring takes precedence over transfer (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

options.text: Arrange short stay ED observation for four hours of fluid resuscitation then discharge if vitals normalise
options.rationale: A four hour observation does not address her severe malnutrition or refeeding risk; medical instability in anorexia nervosa mandates admission rather than brief ED observation (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Admit to a general paediatric or adolescent ward for medical stabilisation with cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding
options.rationale: Multiple ANZAED/RANZCP medical instability criteria are met (bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia below 35.5, potassium below 3.0, phosphate below 0.75, glucose below 3.5); the priority is a monitored medical bed for stabilisation and structured refeeding before any specialist eating disorder placement (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Practice and Treatment Guide for Eating Disorders; NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

explanation.summary: Medical admission in anorexia nervosa is driven by objective instability, not weight alone. ANZAED and RANZCP list bradycardia below 40, postural hypotension with symptomatic drop, hypothermia below 35.5 degrees Celsius, potassium below 3.0 mmol/L, phosphate below 0.75 mmol/L, and hypoglycaemia below 3.5 mmol/L as individually sufficient triggers. Stabilisation happens on the nearest suitable medical or adolescent ward; specialist ED beds follow.
key_points: Any single instability criterion triggers medical admission.
Refeeding syndrome risk peaks in the first 5-7 days; monitor phosphate, potassium, magnesium daily.
Thiamine 100 mg IV or oral before glucose delivery in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: The MARSIPAN threshold of pulse below 40 supine has the highest positive likelihood for imminent cardiac arrhythmia in adolescent anorexia.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19 year old man with a 10 month history of severe restriction. He is currently 44 kg (BMI 14.9) and has been eating around 400 kcal/day for the past three weeks.

He is haemodynamically stable now with pulse 52, blood pressure 104/68 supine to 96/62 standing, temperature 35.9 degrees Celsius. He has no diarrhoea and no recent vomiting.

Admission bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L, glucose 3.9 mmol/L, urea 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, LFTs mildly deranged with ALT 88 U/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52, BP 104/68 supine to 96/62 standing, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 3.6 mmol/L; phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 3.9 mmol/L; ALT 88 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Commence 20 kcal/kg/day divided across three meals with prophylactic oral thiamine and daily electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: Contemporary refeeding guidance in severe restriction starts at around 20 kcal/kg/day (about 900 kcal for this patient), advances every 24-48 hours as electrolytes tolerate, with prophylactic thiamine 100-300 mg daily and daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium monitoring for the first week (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit; RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Start at 5 kcal/kg/day of continuous nasogastric feed with weekly bloods for the first fortnight of admission
options.rationale: 5 kcal/kg/day is below current MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance and risks underfeeding syndrome; the trend has moved to higher starting energy with daily electrolyte checks rather than very low calorie starts (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit).

options.text: Commence 50 kcal/kg/day oral diet from day one with twice weekly electrolytes and no supplements
options.rationale: 50 kcal/kg/day at BMI 14.9 with prolonged restriction risks classical refeeding syndrome with rapid drops in phosphate, potassium and magnesium; energy should be advanced gradually with daily monitoring (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Delay all feeding for 48 hours to correct electrolytes to mid-normal range before offering any calories
options.rationale: Prolonged starvation on the ward worsens catabolism; electrolyte replacement and cautious refeeding should proceed together rather than waiting (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Start intravenous 10% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hour as the sole energy source for the first 72 hours
options.rationale: Intravenous glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in the malnourished, and IV dextrose is not the primary refeeding modality; oral or nasogastric enteral feeding is preferred (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is driven by insulin surge after starvation, causing intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium and expansion of extracellular fluid. Prophylaxis is thiamine before any carbohydrate, staged energy advancement, and daily monitoring in the first week. Australian practice has moved away from ultra-low starting calories toward monitored moderate starts.
key_points: Highest risk: BMI below 14, intake below 500 kcal/day for over a week, prior low electrolytes.
Thiamine 100-300 mg IV or oral before glucose in severe cases.
Daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium for the first 5-7 days.
explanation.pearls: A drop in phosphate to below 0.32 mmol/L in the first 72 hours of refeeding is the hallmark biochemical trigger for refeeding syndrome.

subtopic_detail: EPDS thresholds and next step in perinatal screening
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 32 year old woman at her 6 week postnatal check. Her first baby is feeding well and gaining weight. She reports she has been tearful, waking with anxiety before the baby wakes, and losing interest in things she previously enjoyed.

She has no personal history of mental illness. She has good partner support and does not use alcohol or other substances.

The practice nurse has completed an EPDS today: total score 14 with item 10 (self harm) scored 0. Her previous EPDS at 28 weeks antenatal was 6. There is no evidence of psychotic symptoms, mania, or plans to harm herself or the baby. She is willing to accept help and asks what happens next.

data_table.Screening: EPDS 14/30 today, item 10 score 0; antenatal EPDS at 28 weeks 6/30
data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful; no psychotic features; no thoughts of harm to self or baby

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that a score of 14 is a normal postnatal adjustment reaction and repeat the EPDS in three months
options.rationale: COPE guidance treats EPDS scores of 13 or higher as suggestive of probable depression requiring further assessment, not routine reassurance and delayed repeat screening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).

options.text: Repeat the EPDS in two weeks before making any diagnostic decision, given that a single score is unreliable
options.rationale: COPE and RANZCP recommend acting on a positive EPDS at 13 or above with a diagnostic interview at the same visit rather than delaying two weeks for a repeat screen (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily today as first line for postnatal depression before considering therapy
options.rationale: SSRI monotherapy is appropriate for moderate to severe illness, prior severe episodes, or where therapy is unavailable or declined; psychological therapy is the recommended first line for mild to moderate perinatal depression (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Refer to a mother and baby unit for admission because the EPDS score exceeds the community management cut off
options.rationale: Mother and baby unit admission is reserved for severe depression, postpartum psychosis, or active safety concerns; an EPDS of 14 with no risk features is manageable in the community (Source: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.text: Undertake a structured diagnostic assessment and offer psychological therapy with review in one to two weeks
options.rationale: EPDS 13 or above triggers a full clinical assessment for a mood disorder; first line management of mild to moderate perinatal depression in a woman without prior severe illness is structured psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) with early review, escalating to pharmacotherapy if inadequate response or worsening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is used at every perinatal contact under Australian universal screening. A score of 13 or above indicates probable depression and prompts a diagnostic interview, while any positive response to item 10 mandates immediate risk assessment regardless of total score. Australian first line for mild to moderate perinatal depression is structured psychological therapy with pharmacotherapy for moderate to severe illness.
key_points: EPDS 13+ = probable depression, prompt assessment.
Item 10 above 0 triggers immediate safety review regardless of total.
Sertraline is the preferred SSRI when pharmacotherapy is indicated in breastfeeding.
explanation.pearls: Antenatal EPDS at booking and third trimester and postnatal 6-12 weeks is the COPE-recommended schedule for universal perinatal screening in Australia.

sources.label: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

subtopic_detail: SSRI choice in breastfeeding for moderate postnatal depression
stem:
You are the community perinatal psychiatry registrar seeing a 29 year old woman 9 weeks postnatally. She has moderate depression with early morning waking, anhedonia and pervasive guilt over the past 5 weeks. Two sessions of CBT with the perinatal service have not yet produced improvement.

She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term infant who is thriving. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no active thoughts of self harm.

She took sertraline 50 mg daily during a previous non-perinatal depressive episode 4 years ago with good response and tolerability. She has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications. She is worried about drug transfer into breast milk and wants to continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Examination: Depressed mood; no psychotic features; no thoughts of self harm or infant harm
data_table.Prior response: Sertraline 50 mg daily 4 years ago with good response and no adverse effects
data_table.Breastfeeding: Exclusive breastfeeding; infant thriving on growth chart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice now?

options.text: Commence agomelatine 25 mg orally at night titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
options.rationale: Agomelatine has minimal lactation safety data and requires LFT monitoring; it is not recommended in the perinatal period as a first line antidepressant (Source: AMH).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half life and its active metabolite norfluoxetine accumulates in breastfed infants; sertraline or paroxetine are preferred when initiating an SSRI in a lactating woman (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence citalopram 20 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
options.rationale: Citalopram is compatible with breastfeeding but is not preferred over sertraline when there is a prior positive sertraline response and better infant exposure data for sertraline (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is reserved for treatment resistant depression or as second line where an SSRI trial has failed; it is not first line in a woman with previous SSRI response (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
options.rationale: Sertraline has one of the lowest infant plasma to maternal plasma ratios of the SSRIs, well characterised safety data in breastfeeding, and her prior good response makes it the rational first choice; the RANZCP and eTG both list it as first line for perinatal depression in a woman who wishes to continue breastfeeding (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Sertraline and paroxetine are the SSRIs with the lowest relative infant dose via breast milk and are preferred first line in lactation. Prior good response to a specific SSRI is a strong argument for restarting the same agent given individual pharmacogenomic variability. Continued breastfeeding is compatible with effective maternal treatment and is protective for infant attachment.
key_points: Sertraline: relative infant dose <2%, extensively characterised in breastfeeding.
Avoid fluoxetine at initiation in lactation (long half life, norfluoxetine).
Restart the SSRI that previously worked when tolerability was good.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline's relative infant dose sits around 0.5% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose, well below the 10% conservative safety cut off used in lactation pharmacology.

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis emergency management
stem:
You are the ED registrar called by the community midwife about a 30 year old primiparous woman 12 days postpartum. Over the past 48 hours she has slept 2 hours per night, is speaking rapidly about her baby being sent by God to save the family, and has been overheard saying the baby has divine protection and does not need feeding.

Her partner reports she has been holding the baby at the second story window because angels will catch him if he falls. She has a family history of bipolar I disorder in her mother.

She has no fever and no localising infective signs. Bloods including full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is negative. She refuses admission and says she must remain at home to protect her baby from the doctors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Mental state: Elevated mood, pressured speech, grandiose religious delusions, poor insight; infant safety concerns
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC, TFTs within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Contact child protection to remove the infant and discharge the mother with community mental health follow up
options.rationale: Separating mother and infant is often harmful and unnecessary when a mother and baby unit can safely admit both; child protection notification is a parallel duty but does not replace maternal psychiatric admission (Source: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally daily at home with community follow up in 24 hours by the perinatal team
options.rationale: Community management of postpartum psychosis with active safety concerns and infant risk is unsafe regardless of medication; inpatient care with mother and baby is the standard (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Refer for urgent outpatient psychiatry appointment within 72 hours and arrange for the partner to supervise
options.rationale: Partner supervision cannot substitute for inpatient containment when there is a rapidly evolving psychosis with concrete infant risk behaviours; 72 hour delay is unsafe (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Admit informally to the postnatal ward for observation with midwifery review only and no psychiatric input overnight
options.rationale: Postnatal wards are not equipped for acute psychosis containment; she also lacks capacity to consent to informal admission given active delusional beliefs about the doctors (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Arrange same day involuntary admission under the NSW Mental Health Act to a mother and baby unit or acute psychiatry bed
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with high risk of infant harm and maternal suicide; when the mother refuses voluntary admission, section 19 or 20 scheduling under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 with transfer to a mother and baby unit (or nearest acute psychiatric bed) is indicated (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis has an incidence around 1-2 per 1000 births, peaks in the first 2 weeks postnatally, and carries a suicide rate around 2 per 1000 and infanticide risk around 4%. It is treated as a psychiatric emergency with urgent admission, ideally to a mother and baby unit to preserve the maternal-infant relationship. Family history of bipolar disorder confers up to 20-fold increased risk.
key_points: Emergency admission is the default; involuntary if capacity impaired or refusing.
Prefer mother and baby unit when available; otherwise nearest acute bed.
Antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser typical; ECT for rapid response.
explanation.pearls: Around 20-25% of women with a personal history of bipolar I develop postpartum psychosis after childbirth, making prophylactic lithium in the immediate postpartum period a considered option in specialist care.

sources.label: NSW Health Perinatal and Infant Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Consent and indication for ECT in severe depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on a NSW acute inpatient unit reviewing a 62 year old woman with severe melancholic depression. Over the past 3 weeks she has stopped eating and drinking, has lost 5 kg, and expresses a persistent belief that her internal organs have rotted away.

She has failed adequate trials of two SSRIs and one SNRI over the past 8 months. She is dehydrated and requires IV fluids. Her renal function is preserved and her ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 430 ms.

She accepts admission voluntarily but says she does not want any tablets or any procedures because they will not work. Her son has enduring guardianship for medical decisions. The treating consultant is proposing bilateral ECT under general anaesthesia and asks you to organise consent for the first treatment tomorrow.

data_table.Mental state: Severe melancholic depression; nihilistic delusion of rotted organs; refusing oral intake
data_table.Prior trials: Sertraline 200 mg 8 weeks, escitalopram 20 mg 10 weeks, venlafaxine 225 mg 12 weeks all inadequate
data_table.Investigations: Renal function preserved; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 430 ms; dehydration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate consent pathway to enable ECT tomorrow?

options.text: Proceed under the son's enduring guardianship consent as she has effectively delegated medical decisions to him
options.rationale: In NSW ECT cannot be authorised by a substitute decision maker; the NSW Mental Health Act requires either the patient's own informed consent or an application to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for a specific number of treatments (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Obtain her signed consent tomorrow before the procedure as her refusal today is likely to change overnight
options.rationale: Her nihilistic delusion impairs capacity to weigh risks and benefits, so relying on next-day consent risks proceeding without valid consent; a tribunal pathway is required (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Rely on the doctrine of necessity given the medical risk of continued refusal of oral intake
options.rationale: Emergency ECT in NSW still requires either patient consent, tribunal authorisation, or in a genuine emergency the Chief Psychiatrist's approval; the doctrine of necessity does not itself authorise ECT (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT authorisation given she lacks capacity to consent
options.rationale: Under Chapter 4 Part 2 of the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, where a patient is incapable of consenting to ECT the treating team must apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an order authorising a specific number of treatments; the two consultant certificates support the application (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Defer ECT and continue an eighth week of antidepressant trial while monitoring hydration in hospital
options.rationale: She has already failed adequate trials of three antidepressants and has severe melancholic depression with nihilistic delusions and refusal of intake; ECT is a first line rather than salvage option in this presentation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

explanation.summary: ECT is highly effective for severe melancholic depression, psychotic depression, catatonia, treatment resistant depression, and severe mania. In NSW consent is either given by the patient with capacity or authorised by the Mental Health Review Tribunal on application; substitute decision makers cannot consent to ECT. Two consultant certificates support the application and course length must be specified.
key_points: Response rates 70-90% in melancholic and psychotic depression.
Bilateral ECT is faster but more cognitive impact than right unilateral.
Anaesthetic workup: airway assessment, cardiac and dental review.
explanation.pearls: In NSW the Mental Health Review Tribunal authorises a specified number of ECT treatments (typically up to 12) per application; further courses require reapplication.

subtopic_detail: Cognitive side effects and electrode placement
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 74 year old man three days after his fourth session of bilateral ECT for severe psychotic depression. He is responding well with resolution of nihilistic delusions and improved oral intake.

However he is markedly confused during the day, cannot recall visiting relatives from yesterday morning, and has become disoriented walking back from the bathroom. Baseline cognition was intact with an MoCA of 27 before commencing ECT.

He has no fever, no focal neurology, and no new medications. His electrolytes, glucose, and inflammatory markers are within normal limits. Non contrast CT brain is unchanged from admission. His consultant asks how to modify the ECT plan to preserve response while reducing his cognitive burden.

data_table.Neurology: Confused, poor short term memory recall, no focal signs
data_table.Cognition: MoCA 27 at baseline; not repeated during acute confusion
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, glucose, inflammatory markers within normal limits; CT brain unchanged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate modification to his ECT plan?

options.text: Switch to right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT and continue the treatment course
options.rationale: Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT has substantially less anterograde and retrograde amnesia than bilateral ECT with only modestly slower response; switching modality is the standard response to significant cognitive burden mid-course (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Continue bilateral ECT at current dose and add donepezil 5 mg orally daily to counter cognitive symptoms
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not routine adjuncts during ECT and do not address the mechanism of ECT related cognitive impairment; reducing the cognitive dose of ECT is the first step (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Stop ECT permanently and switch to a trial of ketamine infusion given the cognitive concern
options.rationale: Stopping a working ECT course after only four sessions in a responding psychotic depression risks relapse; modifying to a less cognitively burdensome technique preserves response (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Reduce ECT frequency to weekly at the current bilateral placement and dose per session
options.rationale: Reducing frequency without changing placement does reduce cognitive burden but at the cost of slower recovery in a patient who is now responding; unilateral ultra-brief is a better trade-off (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

options.text: Increase the anaesthetic propofol dose to induce a longer post-ictal recovery and reduce recall of confusion
options.rationale: Higher propofol doses raise seizure threshold and reduce ECT efficacy without addressing the underlying cognitive burden of bilateral stimulation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT).

explanation.summary: Cognitive impairment is the main side effect of ECT and includes acute post-ictal confusion, anterograde amnesia during the course, and variable retrograde amnesia. Older age, bilateral placement, brief pulse (compared with ultra-brief), higher charge, and closer inter-treatment spacing all increase burden. Switching to right unilateral ultra-brief pulse is the primary risk mitigation without abandoning ECT.
key_points: Bilateral fastest response, greatest cognitive impact.
Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse preferred where cognition is a concern.
Retrograde amnesia most often around the course itself and improves over months.
explanation.pearls: Ultra-brief pulse widths (0.3 ms or less) reduce cognitive side effects while maintaining efficacy in most trials of right unilateral ECT.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 34 year old man brought in by ambulance with agitation, sweating and shivering. He is on sertraline 200 mg daily for depression and was started on tramadol 3 days ago after a workplace back injury.

His partner says he took an extra tramadol tablet at 4pm today and became agitated over the next 3 hours. There has been no recent illicit drug use and urine screen is pending.

On examination he is anxious with pressured movements. Pulse 128 regular, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Pupils are 6 mm and reactive. There is spontaneous inducible clonus in both ankles worse on the right, hyperreflexia at knees and ankles, and diaphoretic warm skin. Muscle tone is increased but does not have lead pipe rigidity. Creatine kinase is 220 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Bilateral inducible ankle clonus (right greater than left); hyperreflexia at knees and ankles; increased tone without lead pipe rigidity; pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 220 U/L (30-200); urine drug screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management alongside supportive care?

options.text: Continue current medications, give paracetamol for temperature and observe over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Continuing the precipitating serotonergic combination will worsen the syndrome; paracetamol does not lower hyperthermia driven by increased muscle activity in serotonin syndrome (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add IV dantrolene
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and considered in severe NMS with muscle rigidity; the clonus and hyperreflexia pattern here is serotonin syndrome, where cyproheptadine is the specific antidote (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add oral bromocriptine
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist considered for NMS to counter dopamine blockade; NMS classically causes lead pipe rigidity and much higher CK, not lower limb clonus with hyperreflexia (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add oral cyproheptadine
options.rationale: The clinical picture (lower limb clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, autonomic hyperactivity within hours of adding tramadol to an SSRI) is serotonin syndrome by Hunter criteria; management is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and hyperthermia, and cyproheptadine as a 5-HT2A antagonist for moderate to severe cases (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology; AMH).

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents, give IV haloperidol for agitation and observe temperature response
options.rationale: Haloperidol worsens autonomic instability and is contraindicated for agitation in serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines are the correct sedative (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS share fever, autonomic instability and altered mental state but differ in tempo and neurology. Serotonin syndrome develops within hours of a serotonergic change and features clonus (especially lower limb), hyperreflexia and mydriasis. NMS develops over days on dopamine blockade with lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high CK and normal pupils. Antidotes differ: cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome; bromocriptine and dantrolene for NMS.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia = serotonin syndrome; lead pipe rigidity = NMS.
Hours after serotonergic change vs days on antipsychotic.
Benzodiazepines first for agitation in both; avoid antipsychotics in serotonin syndrome.
explanation.pearls: Tramadol added to any SSRI, SNRI, MAOI or triptan is a leading Australian trigger for serotonin syndrome and appears on the AMH interaction alert list.

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome recognition
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 42 year old man on the psychiatric ward. He was admitted 8 days ago with a first episode of psychosis and started on haloperidol 5 mg twice daily titrated up to 10 mg twice daily 4 days ago.

Over the past 24 hours he has become mute and immobile. Nursing report he was well overnight but reduced oral intake this morning. He is not currently on any other regular medications and has never used antidepressants.

On examination he is diaphoretic. Pulse 118 regular, BP 168/104 fluctuating to 128/78 within minutes, RR 20, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius. He has generalised lead pipe rigidity through all limbs, cogwheeling at the wrists, and hyporeflexia. Pupils are 4 mm equal and reactive. Bloods: creatine kinase 6800 U/L (30-200), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, urea 9.1 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 168/104 fluctuating to 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Mute, diaphoretic; generalised lead pipe rigidity; cogwheeling; hyporeflexia; pupils 4 mm reactive
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 6800 U/L (30-200); WCC 14.2 x10^9/L; urea 9.1 mmol/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue haloperidol at current dose, add procyclidine for extrapyramidal symptoms and give oral paracetamol
options.rationale: Anticholinergics like procyclidine treat drug induced parkinsonism but do not resolve NMS; continuing the antipsychotic is dangerous once NMS is recognised (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease haloperidol, transfer to a monitored bed for IV fluids and cooling, and commence bromocriptine
options.rationale: The picture (recent dose escalation of a high potency D2 blocker, hyperthermia over 38.5, lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, CK over 1000, leucocytosis) is NMS; management is stopping the antipsychotic, aggressive supportive care in a monitored bed, and adding a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine or amantadine (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology; AMH).

options.text: Cease haloperidol, give IV lorazepam for suspected catatonia, and repeat CK in 12 hours before further action
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge is appropriate for catatonia but does not address life threatening hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis; NMS needs immediate supportive care and specific pharmacological reversal (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Cease haloperidol, commence cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, and observe on the psychiatric ward
options.rationale: There are no serotonergic agents on board and the neurology (rigidity with hyporeflexia, not clonus and hyperreflexia) is against serotonin syndrome; cyproheptadine is not the answer (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Continue haloperidol, commence IV dantrolene as monotherapy and manage on the psychiatric ward overnight
options.rationale: Dantrolene is an option in severe rigidity but must be combined with cessation of the antipsychotic and monitored bed level care; the offending drug must always be stopped (Source: eTG Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but life threatening reaction to D2 blockade, most often within the first 2 weeks of starting or escalating a high potency antipsychotic. Mortality is 5-20% mainly from renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis, aspiration, and arrhythmia. Recovery takes 7-10 days after cessation of the offending agent.
key_points: Tetrad: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental state.
Stop the antipsychotic; supportive care in a monitored bed.
Consider bromocriptine, amantadine or dantrolene in severe cases.
explanation.pearls: CK over 1000 U/L in the context of new antipsychotic initiation with fever and rigidity is a diagnostic anchor for NMS in Australian ED practice.

subtopic_detail: CIWA-Ar symptom triggered diazepam regimen
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 52 year old man who normally drinks a bottle of vodka per day. His last drink was 16 hours ago. He is admitted for elective inguinal hernia repair scheduled in 3 days and is on the ward for preoperative alcohol withdrawal management.

He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens in previous withdrawals. He has no chronic liver disease, no cognitive impairment and takes no regular medications.

On examination he is tremulous with mild sweating. Pulse 96 regular, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius. He is oriented, without hallucinations. His CIWA-Ar score is 12 on admission. Bloods including electrolytes, magnesium and glucose are within normal limits, and he has already received parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tremulous, mild sweating, oriented, no hallucinations
data_table.Assessment: CIWA-Ar 12; no prior seizures or delirium tremens; parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV already given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate benzodiazepine regimen now?

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg orally every 6 hours regularly with no CIWA-Ar guided as-needed doses
options.rationale: Lorazepam is reserved for significant hepatic impairment given hepatic first pass; diazepam self-tapers due to long half life and is preferred when liver function is preserved (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally four times daily for 3 days then 5 mg four times daily for 3 days
options.rationale: Fixed schedule benzodiazepines are reserved for patients with prior withdrawal seizures or DTs, unreliable scoring, or where nursing capacity for symptom triggered dosing is limited; symptom triggered is preferred here (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg orally every 2 hours as needed while CIWA-Ar stays at 10 or above
options.rationale: Symptom triggered diazepam titrated to CIWA-Ar (dose typically 10-20 mg orally when score above 10) is the preferred Australian regimen for uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal in patients without prior seizures or DTs, using less total benzodiazepine than fixed schedules and with earlier detection of worsening (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 25 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days without any symptom triggered doses
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide is used in some UK regimens but Australian guidelines prefer diazepam; scheduled dosing without CIWA-Ar risks under or overdosing (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).

options.text: Withhold benzodiazepines until CIWA-Ar reaches 20 then diazepam 10 mg every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: A CIWA-Ar of 12 already meets the threshold for symptom triggered diazepam; waiting to CIWA-Ar 20 delays treatment and risks seizures and DTs (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Symptom triggered diazepam guided by CIWA-Ar is the preferred inpatient regimen for uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal in Australia. Diazepam's long half life provides an inherent taper. Parenteral thiamine (300 mg IV daily for 3-5 days) is given before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Fixed dose regimens are reserved for higher risk patients or where symptom scoring cannot be done reliably.
key_points: Symptom triggered = less total benzodiazepine, shorter withdrawal.
Fixed dose reserved for prior seizures/DTs or unreliable scoring.
Lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment.
explanation.pearls: In NSW the CIWA-Ar action threshold is typically 10; scores above 20 with rising trend or hallucinations should prompt consideration of transfer to a higher acuity bed for delirium tremens.

subtopic_detail: Thiamine and Wernicke prevention in dependent drinking
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 48 year old woman brought in confused after being found in the street. Her partner reports she drinks around 750 mL of spirits daily and eats poorly. Her last drink was 8 hours ago.

She is alert but disoriented to place and time. She has a wide-based gait and nystagmus on lateral gaze bilaterally. She is not febrile and has no focal weakness.

Pulse 108 regular, BP 152/94, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Bloods: sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), glucose 4.8 mmol/L. Non contrast CT brain shows no acute pathology and blood alcohol is 0.12%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 152/94, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Disoriented to place and time; wide-based gait; bilateral lateral gaze nystagmus; no focal weakness
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 137 mmol/L; potassium 3.4 mmol/L; magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 4.8 mmol/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of her thiamine and glucose needs?

options.text: Give IV thiamine 100 mg once daily for 5 days without magnesium replacement and delay any glucose until day 2
options.rationale: 100 mg once daily is inadequate for suspected Wernicke; treatment doses in Australia are 500 mg IV three times daily; magnesium repletion is required for thiamine to function (Source: AMH).

options.text: Give oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily and IV 5% dextrose 1 L over 4 hours to correct suspected hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Oral thiamine has poor bioavailability in dependent drinkers; giving dextrose before adequate parenteral thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Give IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 2-3 days, replace magnesium, and give IV dextrose only after the first thiamine dose
options.rationale: Wernicke encephalopathy is likely (encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia in a chronically undernourished heavy drinker); Australian guidance is high dose parenteral thiamine (500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days then taper), correction of magnesium (a cofactor for thiamine dependent enzymes), and any dextrose given only after the first thiamine dose to avoid precipitating or worsening Wernicke (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine; AMH).

options.text: Withhold thiamine until blood test confirms low thiamine levels and manage confusion with diazepam alone
options.rationale: Serum thiamine is not required to justify treatment; empirical high dose parenteral thiamine is given whenever Wernicke is suspected because the cost of delay is a Korsakoff amnestic syndrome (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Give IM thiamine 100 mg once daily and multivitamin tablet daily and defer magnesium correction to the ward
options.rationale: IM thiamine 100 mg daily is prophylaxis dosing (used in dependent drinkers without Wernicke features), not treatment; her signs meet Wernicke criteria and warrant IV treatment doses (Source: eTG Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy classically presents with any of the triad of encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus, sixth nerve palsy) and ataxia, but only one is needed in a chronically undernourished heavy drinker to justify treatment. IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 2-3 days followed by 250 mg daily and then oral maintenance is the Australian regimen. Magnesium is a cofactor and must be replaced.
key_points: Any one of triad + chronic alcohol use = treat empirically.
Thiamine before any glucose to prevent precipitation.
500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days; taper as symptoms improve.
explanation.pearls: Anaphylactic reactions to IV thiamine occur at rates below 1 per 100 000 doses; resuscitation equipment should be available but the treatment is not withheld for that reason.

subtopic_detail: Buprenorphine-naloxone induction and precipitated withdrawal
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman who has been using illicit oxycodone up to 200 mg per day for 8 months. She is motivated to commence opioid agonist therapy and prefers buprenorphine-naloxone.

Her last oxycodone use was 8 hours ago. She has not previously been on OST. She has no chronic pain condition and no other regular medications. She has no known QT prolongation and hepatitis serology is negative.

On examination she is anxious with mild sweating and yawning. Pulse 92, BP 128/78, pupils 5 mm and reactive. Objective Opioid Withdrawal Scale (OOWS) score is 4 (mild). She asks how quickly you can start buprenorphine-naloxone today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/78, RR 16, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Anxious; mild sweating and yawning; pupils 5 mm reactive; OOWS 4
data_table.History: Illicit oxycodone up to 200 mg/day for 8 months; last dose 8 hours ago; no prior OST

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait until objective withdrawal is at least moderate then give buprenorphine-naloxone 4/1 mg sublingually and titrate
options.rationale: Standard buprenorphine induction requires objective moderate withdrawal (OOWS 5 or above) at least 12 hours after last short acting opioid or 24-48 hours after methadone to avoid precipitated withdrawal, then starting at 4/1 mg with titration by symptom review over the first day (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines; RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Give buprenorphine-naloxone 4/1 mg sublingually now and titrate up to 12/3 mg over 4 hours
options.rationale: Objective withdrawal is still mild (OOWS 4) and short acting opioids clear over 12-24 hours; starting buprenorphine at this point risks precipitated withdrawal because buprenorphine displaces full agonists from the mu receptor (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence; NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Give methadone 40 mg orally now instead as it does not require prior withdrawal to induct safely
options.rationale: Methadone induction starts at 20-30 mg with cautious titration over days because of the risk of accumulation and death during induction; 40 mg is not a safe starting dose and switching against her preference isn't warranted (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Give oral naltrexone 50 mg today and arrange buprenorphine induction after 7 days of abstinence
options.rationale: Naltrexone in an actively opioid dependent user precipitates severe withdrawal and is contraindicated without a fully documented opioid free period of at least 7 days; it is also not aligned with her stated OST preference (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).

options.text: Give sublingual buprenorphine mono product 8 mg now and add naloxone tomorrow to reduce diversion
options.rationale: Combination buprenorphine-naloxone is the preferred agent for community induction because of reduced injection diversion; starting with mono product without indication and delaying until reaching adequate withdrawal is standard, regardless of formulation choice (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial mu agonist that displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal if given too early. NSW OST induction requires objective moderate withdrawal (OOWS 5+ or COWS 12+) at least 12 hours after last short acting opioid or 24-48 hours after methadone. Combination buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred for community use; long acting depot (subcutaneous buprenorphine) is an option once stabilised on sublingual dosing.
key_points: Wait for moderate withdrawal to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
Start 4/1 mg sublingual, review 2 hourly, titrate as needed on day one.
Long acting depot buprenorphine available once stabilised.
explanation.pearls: Sublocade depot buprenorphine (100-300 mg subcutaneously monthly) requires prior stabilisation on transmucosal buprenorphine of at least 8-24 mg/day for 7 days before first depot injection.

sources.label: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Take away doses on methadone maintenance in NSW
stem:
You are the GP registrar in a NSW clinic accredited for OST prescribing. A 39 year old man has been on methadone 80 mg daily for opioid use disorder for 7 months. He attends the pharmacy daily for supervised dosing.

He has been abstinent from illicit opioids and stimulants on random urine drug screens for the past 4 months. He is employed as a plumber, engaged with his GP, and takes no other medications. He has no history of overdose since starting methadone.

He requests two take-away doses per week to make working on outer suburb jobs easier. He has not previously had take-aways. He has a locked medicine box at home and lives alone.

data_table.History: Methadone 80 mg daily for 7 months; 4 months of clean UDS; employed; no overdoses; lives alone with lockable storage
data_table.Assessment: Stable, engaged, no diversion concerns; requesting 2 take-away doses/week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his take-away request?

options.text: Grant four take-away doses per week immediately as he clearly meets the primary NSW stability criteria
options.rationale: NSW OST take-away doses are increased incrementally as stability is demonstrated; jumping straight to four take-aways bypasses the graded pathway and safety review at each step (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Grant two take-away doses per week with documented risk assessment, secure storage plan and structured review
options.rationale: NSW OST guidance allows take-aways on a graded basis once stability is documented (minimum 3 months on methadone for the first take-aways, sustained abstinence from illicit drugs, no diversion risk, adequate storage); starting with 1-2 take-aways per week with structured review is standard (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines; RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Refuse take-away doses because NSW policy prohibits take-aways in the first 12 months of maintenance treatment
options.rationale: There is no 12 month minimum in NSW; the minimum is around 3 months of stable dosing on methadone with the other stability criteria met (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Convert him to buprenorphine-naloxone this week as it allows unsupervised dosing without formal take-away approvals
options.rationale: Buprenorphine-naloxone take-aways still require the same graded stability assessment and NSW OTP approvals; switching a stable methadone patient against his preference for administrative reasons is not appropriate (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Refer to a specialist addiction physician for a subcutaneous depot buprenorphine trial to eliminate his daily pharmacy attendance
options.rationale: Depot buprenorphine is a reasonable long term option but is not the immediate next step for a stable methadone patient asking for a small number of take-aways; his stated preference and current stability support a graded methadone take-away plan (Source: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: Take-away doses in the NSW Opioid Treatment Program balance patient stability and quality of life against risks of diversion, overdose in third parties, and paediatric accidental exposure. Stability criteria include a minimum period on the current dose, negative UDS for illicit substances, absence of diversion or overdose risk, secure storage, and stable social circumstances. Take-aways are increased incrementally with review.
key_points: Minimum around 3 months on methadone before first take-aways.
Start 1-2 take-aways/week; review at each escalation.
Secure lockable storage and safety plan mandatory.
explanation.pearls: NSW OTP allows up to 4 unsupervised methadone take-aways per week for highly stable patients, with any weekly plan requiring specialist consultation and documented dispensing at the authorised pharmacy.

sources.label: NSW Opioid Treatment Program Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: OCD pharmacotherapy first line and dose
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 26 year old woman with obsessive compulsive symptoms for 3 years. She spends about 4 hours per day on contamination checking and hand washing, which now interferes with her Masters coursework.

She has trialled 12 sessions of exposure and response prevention (ERP) with a psychologist over the past 4 months with only partial improvement. She has no bipolar history, no psychotic symptoms, and no active suicidal thoughts.

She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no other medical conditions, does not smoke, drinks alcohol only socially, and takes no regular medications. She is not currently sexually active but has been prescribed the combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation. She is asking about adding a medication to her ERP.

data_table.History: Contamination and washing OCD for 3 years, 4 hours/day rituals; ERP 12 sessions partial response
data_table.Mental state: No bipolar, no psychosis, no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill; no antidepressant history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily, titrated toward 200-300 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: Fluvoxamine is effective in OCD but has substantial CYP interactions (including with the combined oral contraceptive) making it a less convenient first choice; sertraline is preferred here (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily, titrated toward 150-200 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: OCD responds to SSRIs at doses at the upper end of the antidepressant range; sertraline 150-200 mg/day is a first line Australian regimen with a favourable interaction profile in a woman on combined oral contraceptive (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Clomipramine 25 mg orally at night, titrated toward 150-250 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: Clomipramine is effective in OCD but is reserved for SSRI failure due to anticholinergic burden, weight gain, seizure risk at higher doses and ECG monitoring; it is not first line (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily short term while continuing ERP
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have no place in the maintenance treatment of OCD and can undermine ERP by suppressing anxiety exposure; dependence risk over months is significant (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg orally at night added to ongoing ERP as first line augmentation
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation of an SSRI is reserved for OCD that has failed adequate SSRI trials at high dose; using it before any SSRI trial is not appropriate (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

explanation.summary: OCD requires higher SSRI doses and longer trials than depression, typically 10-12 weeks at target dose before deciding response. First line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram) with ERP; clomipramine is second line. Augmentation with low dose risperidone or aripiprazole is considered after failed adequate SSRI trials.
key_points: OCD needs higher SSRI doses (sertraline 150-200 mg, fluoxetine 40-80 mg).
10-12 week trial at target dose before non-response.
ERP is essential; medication supports rather than replaces therapy.
explanation.pearls: The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) is the standard Australian measure of OCD severity and treatment response, with a 25-35% reduction after 10-12 weeks considered a meaningful medication response.

sources.label: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

subtopic_detail: Panic disorder first line SSRI selection and dose ramp
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 33 year old man with recurrent panic attacks over the past 4 months. He has had 3-4 attacks per week with palpitations, chest tightness and a sense of impending doom, plus persistent anticipatory anxiety about further attacks. He has stopped taking public transport.

He has had a normal ECG, TFTs and urine drug screen. He does not use caffeine excessively and drinks alcohol only socially. He is not on any regular medications.

He has agreed to a course of CBT with a psychologist and is asking about medication. He is worried that antidepressants might make his panic worse initially. He has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder and no active suicidal ideation.

data_table.History: Panic attacks 3-4/week for 4 months; agoraphobic avoidance of public transport
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal; TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative
data_table.Mental state: No bipolar features; no active suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial SSRI regimen?

options.text: Alprazolam 0.5 mg orally three times daily as monotherapy with review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Alprazolam causes tolerance, rebound anxiety and dependence in panic disorder and is no longer S8 available in Australia without specialist authority; it is not a first line long term treatment (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily from day one to reach target dose quickly and review at 2 weeks
options.rationale: Starting at 100 mg risks initial anxiety worsening and jitteriness in panic disorder; a low start with slow titration is the recommended approach (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg orally daily for 1 week then increase to 50 mg daily with review at 2 weeks
options.rationale: In panic disorder starting SSRIs at half the usual antidepressant starting dose (sertraline 25 mg, escitalopram 5 mg, fluoxetine 10 mg) reduces the risk of initial anxiety exacerbation; titration to target dose over 2-4 weeks with response assessed at 6-8 weeks is standard (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily as monotherapy for autonomic symptoms with review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Beta blockers may attenuate autonomic symptoms in performance anxiety but do not prevent panic attacks in panic disorder and are not first line monotherapy (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg orally at night as first line pharmacotherapy with review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine can be considered second line in panic disorder, particularly with insomnia or weight loss, but SSRIs are first line with the largest evidence base (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: SSRIs are first line for panic disorder alongside CBT. Starting at low doses and titrating slowly reduces the classic early jitteriness that can otherwise be misattributed by patients to worsening panic and lead to premature discontinuation. Adequate trials require 6-8 weeks at target dose. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short bridging use and are generally avoided due to dependence risk.
key_points: Halve the antidepressant starting dose in panic disorder.
Assess response at 6-8 weeks at target dose.
CBT is at least as effective as medication and durable long term.
explanation.pearls: Alprazolam is a Schedule 8 restricted benzodiazepine in Australia requiring specialist authority; short and intermediate acting benzodiazepines are avoided in panic disorder because of high dependence and rebound risk.

sources.label: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

subtopic_detail: Adult autism spectrum diagnosis in women
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 28 year old woman who suspects she is on the autism spectrum. She has always found social situations exhausting, rehearses conversations before work meetings, and copies expressions from colleagues. She struggles with unexpected changes to her routine and has strong food texture preferences.

She completed a Bachelor of Design and works as a graphic designer. She has been treated for anxiety and depression with sertraline and CBT over 6 years with only partial response. Her older brother has an established autism spectrum disorder diagnosis from childhood.

She scores 34 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-50). Standard developmental screens as a child were reportedly unremarkable and she was described as a quiet, well behaved child. She is asking about the next step in her diagnostic assessment.

data_table.History: Social masking, routine dependence, sensory sensitivities; anxiety and depression only partial response to sertraline and CBT
data_table.Screening: AQ-50 score 34 (cut off 32); AQ-50 subthreshold in childhood
data_table.Family history: Brother with autism spectrum disorder diagnosed in childhood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that her successful career and normal childhood screens exclude autism and continue current mental health treatment
options.rationale: Successful academic and vocational function does not exclude autism, particularly in women who mask; the developmental screens of the era often missed autism in girls and cannot be used to rule out a current diagnosis (Source: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.text: Refer for a specialist multidisciplinary autism assessment using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with a developmental history informant
options.rationale: The RANZCP and Australian Autism Alliance guideline recommends multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment using ADOS-2 (semi-structured observation) and ADI-R (developmental history interview with an informant), particularly important for women who mask; an elevated AQ warrants specialist assessment rather than treatment change (Source: A National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia; RANZCP Position Statement).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.text: Commence methylphenidate for suspected undiagnosed ADHD as it commonly presents this way in adult women
options.rationale: ADHD and autism can co-occur but starting a stimulant without a diagnostic assessment is not appropriate; her presenting features (routine dependence, sensory sensitivities, social masking) are more suggestive of autism than of ADHD (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Diagnose autism spectrum disorder in the room today based on the AQ-50 score above cut off and issue a formal report
options.rationale: The AQ-50 is a screening tool and cannot substitute for structured diagnostic assessment; a positive screen indicates the need for referral, not diagnosis (Source: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis).
source_refs: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

options.text: Switch her sertraline to venlafaxine given anxiety and depression are the primary problem and defer any autism assessment
options.rationale: Deferring diagnostic assessment misses the opportunity to reframe her difficulties, access supports, and tailor mental health care; her AQ-50 warrants specialist assessment now (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Autism).

explanation.summary: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women is under-diagnosed because of camouflaging: internally driven behavioural adaptation that hides autistic traits in social settings. Presentations often include a long history of anxiety and depression with partial treatment response, exhaustion after socialising, routine dependence, sensory sensitivities, and family history. Australian diagnostic pathway is multidisciplinary using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with a developmental informant.
key_points: Masking is common in women and delays diagnosis into adulthood.
AQ-50 is a screen, not a diagnostic tool.
Multidisciplinary assessment includes ADOS-2, ADI-R and informant history.
explanation.pearls: Adult women referred for autism assessment have a mean age at diagnosis around a decade later than men and are more likely to have prior misdiagnoses of borderline personality disorder or treatment resistant depression.

sources.label: National Guideline for Autism Assessment and Diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Conduct disorder versus oppositional defiant disorder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community mental health team seeing a 13 year old boy brought by his mother because of behavioural problems that have escalated over the past 18 months. He has been suspended from school twice this term.

Behaviours over the past year include starting fights that resulted in another student needing sutures, using a knife to threaten a peer during an argument, setting a fire in the bike shed, and staying out overnight three times without contact. Two nights ago the local police returned him after finding him breaking into a shed.

His mother describes him as argumentative and refusing chores since age 7, but says the more serious behaviours started about 18 months ago. He has no diagnosed intellectual disability, no epilepsy, and no substance use disclosed. He shows little remorse for the injuries he has caused.

data_table.History: Fighting causing injury, knife threat, fire setting, staying out overnight, breaking and entering over 18 months
data_table.Longstanding: Argumentative and refusing chores since age 7
data_table.Mental state: Little remorse; no substance use disclosed; no intellectual disability; no epilepsy

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder with intermittent explosive features
options.rationale: ODD centres on angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour and vindictiveness, but does NOT include serious violations of others' rights or major rules; his behaviours have progressed beyond ODD to violations that meet conduct disorder criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Child Adolescent CPG).

options.text: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder with behavioural escalation
options.rationale: DMDD requires chronic severe irritability with frequent temper outbursts in a child before age 10 and is not diagnosed alongside conduct disorder; his hallmark features are rights violations, not sustained irritability (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Conduct disorder, adolescent-onset with limited prosocial emotions
options.rationale: He meets criteria for conduct disorder (aggression to people, destruction of property including fire setting, serious rule violations, deceit/theft over 12 months) with onset of the serious behaviours after age 10 (adolescent onset) and the limited prosocial emotions specifier (lack of remorse); classification directs prognosis and intervention (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Child Adolescent CPG).

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with early adolescent onset
options.rationale: Antisocial personality disorder requires age 18 or older with a prior conduct disorder diagnosis; at 13 he is too young for that diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Substance-induced disruptive behaviour disorder with cannabis use
options.rationale: No substance use has been identified; a substance-induced diagnosis requires temporal linkage to substance use, which is absent here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by repetitive violations of the rights of others or major age appropriate rules across four domains: aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft, and serious rule violations. Childhood-onset (before age 10) and adolescent-onset subtypes have different prognoses, and the limited prosocial emotions specifier identifies a subgroup with a higher risk of persistent antisocial trajectory. Early intervention (parent management training, multisystemic therapy) improves outcomes.
key_points: ODD = defiance and irritability without rights violations.
Conduct disorder = rights and rules violations across 4 domains.
Limited prosocial emotions specifier identifies higher-risk subgroup.
explanation.pearls: Parent management training and multisystemic therapy are the evidence based first line interventions for conduct disorder; pharmacotherapy is reserved for comorbid ADHD, mood disorder, or aggression that has not responded to psychological therapy.

subtopic_detail: First episode psychosis EPPIC pathway referral
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing an 18 year old man brought by his father. Over the past 6 weeks he has withdrawn from friends, stopped attending university lectures, and has become preoccupied with the belief that a particular lecturer is monitoring his thoughts via the campus WiFi.

He describes hearing the lecturer's voice commenting on him at least once a day. He is not agitated and has no plans to harm the lecturer or himself. He has no personal or family history of bipolar or schizophrenia. He does not use cannabis or methamphetamine and urine drug screen is negative.

He is well groomed, calm and cooperative. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination and routine bloods including TFTs, electrolytes and B12 are within normal limits. Non contrast CT brain is unremarkable. He has agreed to review and to accept treatment.

data_table.History: 6 weeks of social withdrawal, delusion of thought monitoring via WiFi, auditory hallucinations of running commentary; no substance use
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; FBC, UEC, TFTs, B12 within normal limits; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that transient psychotic experiences are common in adolescence and review
options.rationale: Six weeks of persistent delusions and daily auditory hallucinations meet the threshold for first episode psychosis, not transient adolescent perceptual experiences; watchful waiting worsens duration of untreated psychosis (Source: Orygen EPPIC Model).

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally at night in general practice and review at four weeks
options.rationale: First episode psychosis is typically initiated on lower doses of atypical antipsychotic (e.g. risperidone 1-2 mg, aripiprazole 5-10 mg) within a specialist early psychosis pathway; olanzapine 10 mg started in primary care alone misses the multidisciplinary components (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Arrange a routine outpatient adult mental health team appointment in eight to twelve weeks
options.rationale: Delay of 8-12 weeks worsens the duration of untreated psychosis, which is a strong predictor of poor long term outcome; urgent early psychosis referral is required (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Refer to a youth focused early psychosis service (headspace Early Psychosis or equivalent) for assessment
options.rationale: First episode psychosis in a young person warrants referral to a youth focused early psychosis program (EPPIC model, delivered in Australia through headspace Early Psychosis and state services), which combines low dose atypical antipsychotic, family involvement, psychosocial intervention and vocational support with better long term outcomes than adult community services (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; Orygen EPPIC Model).

options.text: Arrange involuntary admission under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 for containment and treatment
options.rationale: He is cooperative, has no aggression, no self harm risk, and has agreed to treatment; involuntary admission is not justified when he accepts assessment and treatment via community early psychosis services (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

explanation.summary: The EPPIC (Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre) model, developed at Orygen in Melbourne, is now delivered nationally through headspace Early Psychosis and state early psychosis services. It targets young people aged 12-25 with first episode psychosis, providing low dose antipsychotic, CBT for psychosis, family work, vocational and educational support in the first 2-5 years, when duration of untreated psychosis and outcome are most modifiable.
key_points: Duration of untreated psychosis predicts long term outcome.
EPPIC combines low dose antipsychotic + psychosocial + family + vocational.
Delivered via headspace Early Psychosis and state services.
explanation.pearls: Each additional month of untreated psychosis is associated with worse symptomatic and functional outcomes, driving the emphasis on same-week specialist assessment in the Australian early psychosis pathway.

subtopic_detail: Social and emotional wellbeing framework in Aboriginal mental health
stem:
You are the GP registrar in a regional NSW clinic seeing a 46 year old Aboriginal man for a routine health check. He mentions he has been feeling flat since his uncle died three months ago on Country. He struggles with sleep and has lost interest in football, which he used to coach.

He does not describe hopelessness, has no thoughts of self harm, and drinks alcohol occasionally. He has stable employment and lives with his wife and children. He has not previously accessed mental health care and expresses concern that psychiatric labels might affect his contact with his community.

He would like some help but is unsure what would be appropriate. He asks whether he needs medication and whether he has to see a psychologist in the city. His K10 score today is 21 (moderate distress) and he has no active psychotic symptoms.

data_table.History: Grief over uncle's death 3 months ago; low mood, sleep disturbance, loss of interest in football
data_table.Assessment: K10 score 21 (moderate distress); no psychosis; no self harm; hesitant about mainstream psychiatric care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Refer to an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service or social and emotional wellbeing worker
options.rationale: The social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB) framework recognises connection to Country, family, community and spirituality as central to Aboriginal mental health; first line is culturally safe care through an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service or SEWB worker, with mainstream referrals offered alongside rather than instead of that pathway (Source: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing; RACGP National Guide).
source_refs: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing
RACGP National Guide to a preventive health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily today given his K10 of 21 indicates moderate distress
options.rationale: His current presentation is culturally embedded grief with mild-moderate distress and no depression diagnosis established; starting an SSRI without offering culturally safe support first bypasses the primary framework and his stated concerns (Source: RACGP National Guide).
source_refs: RACGP National Guide to a preventive health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

options.text: Reassure him that grief is normal, no intervention is needed and review him again in six months
options.rationale: He has asked for help and has moderate distress on the K10; watchful waiting for 6 months without offering support risks worsening and misses the opportunity for culturally aligned early intervention (Source: National Strategic Framework SEWB).
source_refs: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing

options.text: Refer to metropolitan psychiatry services for formal DSM diagnostic assessment before any support
options.rationale: A metropolitan referral misses local culturally safe options and adds barriers for a client already ambivalent about mainstream services; local ACCHS pathways are the primary door (Source: National Strategic Framework SEWB).
source_refs: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing

options.text: Arrange voluntary admission to the acute psychiatric unit for containment given his bereavement
options.rationale: There is no clinical indication for admission (no risk, no psychosis, moderate distress only) and admission is likely to erode trust and worsen engagement (Source: RANZCP position on cultural safety).
source_refs: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing

explanation.summary: The social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB) framework, articulated in the National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing, situates mental health within connection to body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, Country, and spirituality. Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services and SEWB workers provide culturally safe care. Mainstream services are offered alongside rather than as substitutes.
key_points: SEWB extends beyond individual mood to family, culture and Country.
ACCHS and SEWB workers are the primary door to care.
Cultural safety is a clinical safety issue, not an add-on.
explanation.pearls: The Kessler K10 has been adapted for use in Aboriginal populations as the K5 and aK10 with revised cut offs in some communities; local ACCHS teams can guide interpretation and follow up in that context.

sources.label: National Strategic Framework for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Mental Health and Social and Emotional Wellbeing
RACGP National Guide to a preventive health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

subtopic_detail: SSRI failure in generalised anxiety disorder augmentation choice
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 42 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder for 3 years. She has had adequate trials of escitalopram 20 mg daily for 12 weeks and then sertraline 200 mg daily for 12 weeks with only a 20% reduction in her GAD-7 score.

She has also completed a 16 session CBT program with a psychologist during the sertraline trial. She has ongoing pervasive worry, muscle tension and initial insomnia. She works as a solicitor and drives to work daily. She has no history of substance use disorder and no bipolar features.

She has never had a benzodiazepine. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 445 ms. Renal and hepatic function are within normal limits. She takes no other regular medications and does not smoke. She is asking about the next step in medication.

data_table.History: GAD 3 years; failed escitalopram 20 mg 12 weeks; failed sertraline 200 mg 12 weeks; 16-session CBT during sertraline trial
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 445 ms; renal and hepatic function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Add quetiapine 25 mg orally at night, titrated to 150-300 mg/day as SSRI augmentation
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation with quetiapine has evidence in GAD but carries metabolic and cardiometabolic risk; it is reserved for treatment resistant cases after switching class first (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily long term as SSRI augmentation for residual anxiety
options.rationale: Long term benzodiazepine augmentation of an SSRI in GAD risks dependence and impairs driving and legal work; benzodiazepines are used only for short bridging (weeks) rather than sustained augmentation (Source: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Add pregabalin 75 mg orally twice daily, titrated to 300-600 mg/day divided doses as SSRI augmentation
options.rationale: Pregabalin is an option in GAD but is not first choice after two failed SSRIs in Australia; it also carries misuse potential and dose-dependent cognitive/driving effects, and is not PBS listed for GAD (Source: AMH).

options.text: Switch to venlafaxine XR 75 mg orally daily, titrated toward 150-225 mg/day over 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: After failure of two adequate SSRI trials in GAD, the next line is switching to an SNRI (venlafaxine XR or duloxetine); venlafaxine XR is well studied in GAD with dose-response up to 225 mg/day, is compatible with her occupation and driving, and avoids the sedation and dependence risks of the alternative options (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily as SSRI augmentation for somatic anxiety symptoms
options.rationale: Beta blockers attenuate autonomic symptoms in acute situations (e.g. performance anxiety) but do not treat the cognitive core of GAD and are not an evidence-based augmentation strategy after SSRI failure (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: GAD treatment ladder in Australia is CBT and/or an SSRI first line; on inadequate response after 8-12 weeks at target dose, either switch SSRI or switch class to an SNRI (venlafaxine XR, duloxetine). Third line options include pregabalin, buspirone, or antipsychotic augmentation. Benzodiazepines are used only for short bridging in acute severe anxiety, not as sustained augmentation.
key_points: Adequate trial = 8-12 weeks at target dose.
Class switch (SSRI to SNRI) after two failed SSRIs is standard.
Benzodiazepines are short bridging only, not maintenance.
explanation.pearls: Venlafaxine XR shows a dose-response relationship in GAD up to 225 mg/day with an approximate 50% response rate in SSRI failures, though blood pressure needs monitoring at doses above 150 mg/day.

sources.label: RANZCP Anxiety and Related Disorders CPG
